scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #5092: PC1 (10.1.0.100) can ping the corporate gateway and Office-B
internal devices fine, and DNS resolves names, but no TCP connection to any
public Internet server completes -- they all time out. The outage started
around the time of an ISP maintenance notice, so the network team is convinced
the ISP (ISPA) dropped our circuit and wants us to open a fault ticket with
ISPA. Please confirm the ISP-side outage so we can escalate to the carrier.
scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath1-r1-nat-flushed: r1's iptables nat
POSTROUTING chain has been flushed, so its MASQUERADE rules are gone. r1 is the
NAT boundary for all internal /24 subnets (A-PC, B-PC, A-Mgmt, B-Mgmt, Wi-Fi).
Without MASQUERADE, outbound packets from 10.x leave r1's WAN interface with
their RFC1918 source addresses unchanged; ISPA's ACL 100 silently drops RFC1918
source ranges at the WAN edge, so the connections time out with no reply.
Internal traffic is unaffected because it never crosses r1.

The TWIST: the ticket blames the ISP and wants a carrier escalation. The ISP
link and egress are FINE -- this is a local NAT failure on r1, not a circuit
outage. The "Internet down" framing plus an ISP maintenance notice is a
coincidence/red herring; ISPA is doing exactly what its policy says (dropping
unNATed RFC1918 sources), which is the expected behaviour for correctly-NATed
traffic and is not a fault. Decisive tells that the WAN is up: r1's default
route is present and its OSPF/WAN adjacency to ISPA is intact, and traffic
that IS correctly translated (or r1's own sourced traffic) would egress
normally -- only the internal 10.x hosts, whose NAT was removed, are affected.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = r1 (iptables nat
POSTROUTING MASQUERADE rules missing). The agent must localize from the NAT
evidence and explicitly NOT escalate to ISPA / NOT confirm an ISP outage. An
agent that "confirms the ISP circuit is down" has followed the accusation
instead of the evidence. Fix: re-add the MASQUERADE rules on r1 (re-run the
relevant block from r1.startup).
scenario.fix_spec:
re-add MASQUERADE rules for each internal subnet via
  iptables, or re-run the relevant block from r1.startup.
scoring_axes: must-identify-nat-missing: NAT / iptables nat POSTROUTING / MASQUERADE rules flushed on r1

bonus-isp-link-fine: exonerates the ISP side by any verified mechanism -- e.g. the WAN link/egress is healthy and unmasqueraded RFC1918 sources cannot return (whether described as ISPA ingress policy or as the ISP having no route back to 10.0.0.0/8)

agent.diagnosis_text:
The root cause is the complete absence of all outbound NAT (MASQUERADE) rules on
the border router r1. The device's startup script (r1.startup, Section D) defines
ten iptables POSTROUTING MASQUERADE rules — one for each of five internal subnets
(10.1–10.6.0.0/24) egressing via each of the two ISP uplinks (eth2/ISPA,
eth3/ISPB). In the live running state, none of these rules are present:
iptables-save shows an empty POSTROUTING chain with only the DNAT inbound
port-forward for 203.0.113.113→10.5.0.4 remaining.

Without NAT, packets from PC1 (10.1.0.100) are forwarded toward ISPA with their
private RFC-1918 source address intact. ISPA's routing table carries no route to
any 10.x.x.x prefix, so it cannot deliver return traffic — SYN packets egress but
SYN-ACK packets are never routed back. This produces silent timeout failures for
all TCP sessions (and in fact for any protocol, including ICMP to public IPs:
PC1's ping to 8.8.8.8 shows 100% loss). Internal reachability is unaffected
because intra-campus flows never traverse the NAT boundary. DNS succeeds only
because the nameserver is the internal host at 10.5.0.4.

The ISP circuit itself is entirely healthy: r1 reaches ISPA (203.0.113.1) and
ISPB (203.0.113.5) with zero loss. The "ISP maintenance" narrative is a red
herring.

Corrective fix: restore the ten missing MASQUERADE rules on r1, e.g.:
  iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.1.0.0/24 -o eth2 -j MASQUERADE
  iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.1.0.0/24 -o eth3 -j MASQUERADE
(repeat for 10.2–10.6.0.0/24) and also restore the SNAT for the public DNS
server: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.5.0.4 -j SNAT --to-source
203.0.113.113.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-nat-missing: NAT / iptables nat POSTROUTING / MASQUERADE rules flushed on r1
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly identifies that r1's iptables nat POSTROUTING MASQUERADE rules are missing/flushed and cites iptables-save showing an empty POSTROUTING chain.

per_axis.axis: bonus-isp-link-fine: exonerates the ISP side by any verified mechanism -- e.g. the WAN link/egress is healthy and unmasqueraded RFC1918 sources cannot return (whether described as ISPA ingress policy or as the ISP having no route back to 10.0.0.0/8)
per_axis.rationale: Yes — the writeup explicitly verifies the WAN is healthy (reachability to ISPA/ISPB) and explains that un-NATed RFC1918 sources cannot get return traffic (ISP has no route/ingress policy), exonerating the ISP.
Correctly recommends re-adding the missing POSTROUTING MASQUERADE rules (and restoring the DNS SNAT), which matches the expected fix.

The log records show r1's NAT rules are missing, r1's WAN adjacencies are up, and internal host egress fails — the agent's conclusion that missing MASQUERADE on r1 causes the outage follows directly and the essential checks were performed. Minor truncations of command outputs remain, but the agent's key claims are supported by observed command results and pings.
